name: RBI Grade B
fullName: Reserve Bank of India – Officers in Grade 'B' (DR) General: Phase I
eligibility: Graduate with ≥60% (55% for SC/ST/PwBD) or post-graduate with ≥55% (pass for SC/ST/PwBD); 21–30 years (relaxations apply); limited number of attempts for the General stream

notification.summary: The 2026 cycle (≈60 posts: ≈40 General, ≈10 DEPR, ≈10 DSIM as reported) is in its final stage: Phase I for the General stream was held on 13 Jun 2026 and Phase II on 25 Jul 2026; the Phase II result/interview shortlist was reported in Aug 2026 and the final result was awaited in late Sep 2026. The next notification is expected around Apr–May 2027. Dates are from education portals; the RBI site could not be opened from the research environment.

pattern.notes: Sectional timing (approx.): GA 25 min, Reasoning 45 min, English 25 min, Quant 25 min. Sectional and aggregate cut-offs apply; Phase I is qualifying only. Phase II has three papers (Economic & Social Issues, English writing, Finance & Management) followed by an interview (Phase II + interview decide the merit).

trendAnalysis.summary: Phase I is moderate overall; reasoning (puzzles of 5–6 sets: square/circular tables, box, floor, year/age-based) is the most time-consuming and was rated moderate-to-difficult in 2026. GA carries 80 marks and is dominated by 6–8 months of current affairs on banking, RBI policy, economy, government schemes, international reports and appointments; static questions are few. Quant is DI-heavy (missing-data tables, caselets) and in 2026 swapped quadratic equations for simplification/approximation. English (RC, cloze, error spotting, fillers, para-jumbles) was easier than 2025. Overall good attempts were reported around 100–115 with cut-offs near 100 ± 5.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from memory-based analyses of RBI Grade B (General) Phase I 2024 (Sept 2024) and 2025 (18 Oct 2025) published by coaching sites (Bankersadda, PracticeMock, C4S Courses, Mahendras), cross-checked against the official Phase I pattern (GA 80, Reasoning 60, English 30, Quant 30). GA archetypes are framed around recurring themes (RBI Act provisions, regulatory circulars, payment systems, schemes, reports) rather than specific current-affairs items. Patterns are paraphrased; no real question is reproduced.

archetypes.pattern: RC set (450–600 words) on monetary policy, banking or the economy: central idea / author's main concern; distractors are partial or overstated claims
RC fact-check: 'Which of the following is true / NOT true according to the passage' — one option distorts a qualifier (some→most, may→will) or reverses cause and effect
RC inference with statements I, II, III and combination options (Only I / Only I and III …); the trap statement overstates what the passage says
RC vocabulary-in-context: synonym or antonym of a word used in the passage, with distractors that are dictionary meanings not fitting the context
Passage cloze with numbered blanks; five same-part-of-speech options where distractors are look-alike or collocation-breaking words
Sentence split into parts (A)–(D) plus 'No error' (E); errors in subject–verb agreement, prepositions, pronouns, tense, comparatives, or inversion after negative adverbs
Choose the grammatically correct (or incorrect) sentence among five similar sentences on one theme
Double filler: two blanks in one sentence, five word-pairs where one word of each wrong pair fits but the other does not
Single filler: one blank, five words close in meaning; only one matches the tone/collocation of the sentence
Para jumble of five or six sentences on one theme; choose the correct order (options are sequences); connectors like 'however', 'as a result' and pronouns fix the order
Para jumble asking which sentence comes FIRST / THIRD / LAST after rearrangement (options are sentence letters)
Standalone synonym/antonym of a moderately advanced word; distractors include words of the opposite sense
Meaning of an idiom/phrasal verb used in a sentence; distractors are literal readings
Table DI (5 rows × 2–3 columns): percentage increase/decrease of one entity between two years, or one entity as a percentage of another

Caselet DI: a paragraph giving a total and splits in ratios/percentages; questions combine two splits or ask what changes after a transfer
Pie-chart DI (shares in % or degrees of a total): find values, differences and ratios across sectors
Bar/line-graph DI (values given for 5–6 categories or months): averages, ratios and percentage differences
Two quadratic equations in x and y with integer/fraction roots; compare x and y using the five standard relations (> ≥ < ≤ / cannot be established)
Missing number series built on differences of squares/cubes, alternate ×n +k, or ×n with increasing n
Approximation: decimals close to whole numbers in %, ×, ÷, √ and powers; find the nearest value
Arithmetic word problem on profit & loss / discount with two-step conditions
Time & work / pipes: efficiencies combined, one leaves after some days, or an emptying pipe

Point-based direction: several points given relative to each other; find direction/distance between two of them

questions.question:
Eight persons J, K, L, M, N, O, P and Q sit around a square table. Four sit at the four corners facing the centre and four sit at the middle of the four sides facing away from the centre. J sits at a corner. Q sits third to the left of J. N sits opposite J. M sits immediately to the right of J. K is an immediate neighbour of N and faces away from the centre. O faces away from the centre. L is not an immediate neighbour of M. Only one person sits between N and P.

Who sits second to the right of K?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from J (corner): J, O, L, Q, N, K, P, M. Corner-sitters face the centre (right = anticlockwise); side-sitters face outward (right = clockwise). K faces outward, so second to its right (clockwise) is M.

The number of boxes above V is equal to the number of boxes below P. Q is kept immediately below V. R is kept somewhere above U, and only one box is kept between R and S. W is kept adjacent to Q.

How many boxes are kept between W and U?

questions.question:
Eight boxes P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W are kept one above another (position 1 is the bottom, 8 the top). Only three boxes are kept between P and T. T is kept at one of the two lowest positions. The number of boxes above V is equal to the number of boxes below P. Q is kept immediately below V. R is kept somewhere above U, and only one box is kept between R and S. W is kept adjacent to Q.

Which box is kept immediately above P?
questions.explanation: If T = 1, P = 5; boxes above V = boxes below P = 4, so V = 4 and Q = 3; W adjacent to Q is 2. R above U with one box between R and S gives S = 6, U = 7, R = 8. (T = 2 leads to a contradiction.) S is immediately above P.

questions.question:
Statements: Only a few banks are lenders. All lenders are institutions. No institution is a broker.
Conclusions: I. Some banks are not brokers. II. Some brokers are lenders.
questions.explanation: Banks that are lenders are institutions and hence not brokers — I follows. No lender (an institution) can be a broker — II is false.

relevance.note: Only-a-few chain with 'Some banks are not brokers'

questions.question:
Statements: All coins are notes. Some notes are cheques. No cheque is a draft.
Conclusions: I. Some coins being drafts is a possibility. II. No note is a draft.
questions.explanation: Coins are notes, and notes that are not cheques may be drafts, so coins being drafts is possible — I follows. Some notes may be drafts, so II is not definite.

questions.question:
Statements: P ≥ Q > R ≤ S; T > Q ≥ U
Conclusions: I. T > R  II. P ≥ U
questions.explanation: T > Q > R gives T > R; P ≥ Q ≥ U gives P ≥ U. Both follow.

relevance.note: Two-statement inequality both follow; light for RBI

questions.question:
Statements: A ≤ B < C = D; E > D ≥ F; G ≥ E
Conclusions: I. G > B  II. F < C
questions.explanation: G ≥ E > D = C > B gives G > B. F ≤ D = C gives only F ≤ C, so 'F < C' is not definite. Only I follows.

questions.question: In a family, L is the mother of M. M is married to N. O is the son of N. P is the sister of O. Q is the father of N. R is the wife of Q. How is R related to P?
questions.explanation: N is the child of Q and R. O and P are N's children. So R is P's grandmother.

questions.question: Point A is 12 m east of point B. Point C is 5 m north of A. Point D is 4 m west of C. Point E is 11 m south of D. How far and in which direction is E from B?
questions.explanation: Take B = (0,0): A = (12,0), C = (12,5), D = (8,5), E = (8,−6). Distance = √(8² + 6²) = 10 m, towards the South-East.

questions.question:
Statement: An advertisement says, 'Use our UPI app — zero charges on all transfers.'
Assumptions: I. People prefer not to pay charges on money transfers. II. No other app offers zero-charge transfers.
options: Either I or II is implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit
questions.explanation: The advertisement assumes zero charges will attract users (I is implicit). It does not assume that no competitor offers the same (II is not implicit).

questions.explanation: With 'not only … but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the manager' (singular): 'was surprised'. Error in part B.

questions.question:

II. y² + 8y + 15 = 0

questions.question: A, B and C can finish a job in 10, 12 and 15 days respectively. All three start together, but A leaves after 2 days. In how many days in total is the job completed?
questions.explanation: Per day (in 60ths): A 6, B 5, C 4. First 2 days: 2 × 15 = 30/60. Remaining 30/60 at 9/60 per day = 10/3 days. Total = 2 + 3⅓ = 5⅓ days.

questions.question: Under the RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility, the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate serves as:
options: The upper bound (ceiling) of the policy rate corridor
The lower bound (floor) of the policy rate corridor
The rate at which the RBI absorbs surplus liquidity overnight
The rate of interest paid on banks' CRR balances
questions.explanation: MSF is the rate at which banks can borrow overnight against excess SLR securities in emergencies; it forms the ceiling of the LAF corridor, while the Standing Deposit Facility rate is the floor.

questions.question: Banks in India maintain the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) under which provision?
options: Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
questions.explanation: SLR is prescribed under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Section 42 of the RBI Act covers CRR; Section 45ZB the MPC; Section 35A the RBI's power to give directions.

questions.question: Which Basel III requirement obliges banks to hold enough high-quality liquid assets to meet net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period?
questions.explanation: The LCR covers a 30-day stress horizon. The NSFR looks at stable funding over one year; the leverage ratio and capital buffers concern capital, not liquidity.

questions.question: Under the Basel III capital framework as implemented by the RBI for scheduled commercial banks, the Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB) is:
questions.explanation: The CCB, to be held in Common Equity Tier 1, is 2.5% of RWAs (fully phased in from October 2021). 5.5% is the minimum CET1 ratio and 9% the minimum total CRAR in India.

questions.question: Under the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025, a depositor can nominate up to how many persons for a deposit account?
questions.explanation: The 2025 amendment allows up to four nominees for deposit accounts, either simultaneously (in specified shares) or successively.

relevance.note: Four nominees under 2025 amendment (in force Nov 2025); recent enough

questions.question: In India, the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) is compiled and released by:

questions.explanation: WPI is released by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT. The NSO compiles CPI and IIP; the Labour Bureau compiles CPI for industrial workers.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

For decades, Indian households kept the bulk of their savings in bank deposits, gold and property. That pattern is changing. Monthly contributions to mutual funds through systematic investment plans have climbed steadily, and the number of individual investors with demat accounts has multiplied. Optimists see this as a sign of financial deepening: savings that once lay idle in gold or were locked into real estate are being channelled into companies that need capital to grow.

The shift, however, carries risks that are easy to overlook in a rising market. Many new investors have never experienced a prolonged downturn, and surveys suggest that a significant share expect returns far above what equities have historically delivered. If prices fall sharply, disappointed savers may withdraw in panic, crystallising losses and souring an entire generation on markets. Banks face a quieter challenge: as deposits grow more slowly than loans, they must either raise deposit rates, which squeezes their margins, or rely on costlier wholesale funding.

None of this argues for reversing the trend. A household sector that participates in capital markets can make an economy more resilient, provided participation rests on understanding rather than exuberance. Regulators have therefore emphasised suitability — ensuring that products sold to an investor match that person's needs and capacity to bear risk — alongside clearer disclosure of costs and past performance.

Which of the following best expresses the author's main argument?
options: Households should return to bank deposits and gold because markets are too risky
The movement of household savings into markets is welcome, but it must rest on investor understanding while its side-effects on banks are managed
Rising mutual fund inflows have solved the funding problems of Indian banks
Regulators should restrict new investors from entering the equity market
Equity returns in India have always exceeded investors' expectations
questions.explanation: The author calls the shift 'financial deepening', warns of investor over-optimism and bank funding pressure, and concludes that participation must rest on understanding — not that it should be reversed or restricted.

relevance.note: Household-savings shift passage main argument; RBI-faithful theme and traps

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's main concern in the passage?
options: ECL will eliminate the boom-and-bust cycles of Indian banking.
ECL is an improvement on incurred-loss provisioning, but its benefits depend on sound data, models and supervision.
The incurred-loss approach should be retained because ECL relies too much on judgment.
Smaller lenders lack data and should therefore be exempted from ECL.
The one-time jump in provisions under ECL will wipe out the capital of most banks.
questions.explanation: The author supports the shift ('None of this is an argument for retaining the old system') but stresses that ECL is 'only as good as the data, models and governance behind it'. The other options overstate ('eliminate', 'wipe out'), reverse the author's view, or add a recommendation the passage never makes.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is true?
options: Under ECL, every loan must be provided for over its entire remaining life from the day of disbursement.
International experience proves that forward-looking provisioning prevents banking crises.
Regulators usually require the entire transition impact of ECL to be absorbed in the first year.
Under the incurred-loss approach, provisions tend to rise sharply when the economy turns down.
Two banks with similar loan books will report nearly identical provisions under ECL.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Provisions rise sharply just when the economy turns down'. Lifetime provisioning applies only to loans whose risk has increased significantly; experience offers 'some support', not proof; the impact is commonly spread over a few years; and similar banks 'may arrive at quite different provisions'.

I. A bank that expands its loan book rapidly would have to make provisions earlier under ECL than under the incurred-loss approach.
II. Smaller lenders will be required to adopt ECL before large banks do.
III. Some banks have so far invested in risk management mainly to satisfy regulatory requirements.
questions.explanation: I follows from 'a lender that grows its loan book aggressively … will be forced to recognise the risk' from the day of disbursement. questions.question: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'perverse' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: The outcome is 'perverse' because a rule meant to be prudent ends up cutting lending when credit is most needed — i.e. counterproductive. 'Wicked' and 'stubborn' are dictionary senses of 'perverse' that do not fit an outcome.

questions.question: Which of the following is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word 'scrutinise' as used in the passage?

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage as a feature or consequence of the ECL framework?

It allows banks to stop classifying overdue loans as non-performing.
Its first application usually requires a one-time jump in provisions.
Its outcomes depend heavily on models and the assumptions banks choose.
questions.explanation: The passage says nothing about ECL ending NPA classification; the remaining four statements appear in paragraphs 2 and 4.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Digital lending should be stopped because it encourages consumption rather than asset creation.
Regulators have unfairly penalised responsible borrowers by raising capital requirements.
Easy digital credit has widened access but raised the risk of over-borrowing, calling for early regulation and better financial literacy.
India's household debt is too low by international standards and should be allowed to rise.
High interest rates fully compensate lenders for losses on small-ticket loans.
questions.explanation: The passage traces the benefits and risks of the unsecured-credit boom and ends by recommending timely regulation plus financial literacy. The other options are either extreme or present a view the author reports (critics, lenders' assumption) as the author's own.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is true?

India's household debt is high by international standards relative to national income.
Higher capital requirements have stopped credit growth in unsecured segments.

questions.question: Which of the following is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word 'prudent' as used in the passage?

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (2)?

acting to prevent a problem only after the damage has already been done
allowing a problem to continue without any action

passages.title: Reading comprehension: expected credit loss provisioning
passages.text:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it.

For decades, banks in India have set aside money for bad loans only after the damage was visible. Under the incurred-loss approach, a loan is provided for once it has been overdue for ninety days and classified as non-performing. The logic is straightforward — banks should not be asked to provide for losses that have not yet happened — but the outcome has often been perverse. Provisions rise sharply just when the economy turns down, eating into capital at the very moment banks most need it to keep lending. Losses that were building up quietly in good times appear on balance sheets all at once, and lending contracts when credit is scarcest.

The expected credit loss (ECL) framework, which Indian regulators are preparing to introduce, attempts to reverse this sequence. Instead of waiting for a default, a bank must estimate, from the day it disburses a loan, the probability that the borrower will fail to pay and the loss it would suffer if that happened. Loans are placed in stages: those performing as expected carry a provision for losses likely in the next twelve months, while those whose credit risk has increased significantly must be provided for over their entire remaining life. Provisions thus begin to rise when warning signs appear, rather than after the borrower has stopped paying.

Supporters argue that the change will make bank balance sheets more honest. A lender that grows its loan book aggressively in a boom will be forced to recognise the risk it is taking on, which should discourage reckless expansion. Because provisions are built up gradually, the shock of a downturn would also be smaller. International experience offers some support: banks that adopted forward-looking provisioning earlier tended to recognise problem loans sooner.

The transition, however, is far from painless. The first application of ECL usually requires a one-time jump in provisions, which can dent the capital of weaker banks; regulators commonly allow this impact to be spread over a few years for precisely this reason. More fundamentally, the framework depends heavily on models and judgment. Estimating the probability of default requires long, reliable data on borrower behaviour, which smaller lenders often do not possess. Two banks with similar loan books may arrive at quite different provisions simply because their assumptions differ, and a bank under pressure to report profits may be tempted to choose optimistic assumptions.

None of this is an argument for retaining the old system. It is, rather, a reminder that ECL provisioning will be only as good as the data, models and governance behind it. Supervisors will need to scrutinise not just the final numbers but the reasoning that produced them, and banks will need to invest in risk-management capacity that many have so far treated as a mere compliance cost. If they do, the reform could make Indian banking less prone to the boom-and-bust cycles that have repeatedly strained it.

passages.title: Reading comprehension: the rise of unsecured household credit
passages.text:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it.

Over the past few years, borrowing by Indian households has changed in both size and character. Where home loans once dominated, a growing share of new credit now takes the form of personal loans, credit-card balances and small-ticket loans offered at the click of a button. For many young earners, a loan approved within minutes on a phone is their first encounter with formal credit, and the convenience has undeniably widened access.

The speed that makes digital lending attractive, however, also makes it easy to borrow more than one can repay. Small loans are frequently taken to meet routine consumption rather than to build assets, and borrowers often hold several such loans from different lenders at the same time. Because each lender sees only part of the picture, the total burden on an individual can grow unnoticed until a single shock — a lost job or a medical bill — tips the borrower into default. Delinquencies in some small-ticket segments have already risen faster than in the loan book as a whole.

Lenders have responded in contrasting ways. Some have tightened approvals and cut back on the smallest, riskiest loans; others, chasing growth, have continued to lend on the assumption that high interest rates will compensate for higher losses. That assumption may hold for a single lender in good times, but it breaks down when many lenders serve the same over-stretched borrowers, since a default to one is soon followed by defaults to all.

Regulators have therefore preferred to lean against the build-up early rather than wait for a crisis. Raising the capital that lenders must hold against unsecured consumer loans makes such lending costlier and nudges lenders to price risk more carefully. Requiring lenders to report credit information more frequently helps each of them see a borrower's full obligations. Such measures inevitably slow credit growth in the affected segments, and critics argue that they penalise responsible borrowers along with reckless ones.

The deeper issue is that household debt in India, though low by international standards when measured against national income, is concentrated among borrowers with modest and uncertain earnings. For them, what matters is not the aggregate ratio but the share of monthly income consumed by repayments. A prudent approach would combine timely regulation with better financial literacy, so that the gains of easy credit are not undone by its costs.
